title: The Cost of Waiting
eyebrow: CETI · the 75-second case · cost of delay
lede: “We'll start with the biggest project; the small ones can wait.” Three features, one team, six months: count what the waiting costs under each order, then see why the cheapest-looking plan is not.

commit.title: YOUR NUMBER
commit.prompt: Biggest first, as planned. Six months: what does the waiting cost in total, in £k?

chapters.eyebrow: COST OF DELAY · THE CASE · MAERSK LINE
chapters.title: One feature, waiting

captions: “Start with the biggest. The small ones can wait.”
Three features. Each earns only once it ships.
Biggest first. Seal a number: what does waiting cost?
Maersk Line: one feature, 82 hours of work.
It took 46 weeks to ship. 38 were spent waiting.
Each week of waiting: over $200,000 not earned.
Your three. One mark: £50k not yet earned, per month.
Reordered: 24 marks. £1.2M. Same work, same team.
The rule: £ a month ÷ months of work. Highest first.
Monday: what does a month of delay cost, for each item?
Teaching numbers. Real cost of delay is an estimate.
ledger: REV C · THE CASE: MAERSK LINE

brand.takeaway: Do first what loses the most per month of work.

sources: Reinertsen, D. G. The Principles of Product Development Flow: Second Generation Lean Product Development. Celeritas Publishing, 2009. Cost of delay (“If you only quantify one thing, quantify the cost of delay”); Weighted Shortest Job First = cost of delay ÷ duration.

Arnold, J. J. & Yüce, Ö. “Black Swan Farming Using Cost of Delay: Discover, Nurture and Speed Up Delivery of Value.” Agile Conference 2013 (AGILE 2013), IEEE, pp. 101–116. doi:10.1109/AGILE.2013.16. Maersk Line, a portfolio of about $100M; CD3 = cost of delay divided by duration.

Arnold, J. J. “Cost of Delay.” Black Swan Farming, blackswanfarming.com/cost-of-delay: the Maersk feature, about 82 hours of work, 46 weeks idea to launch, over 38 weeks in queues, more than $200,000 per week, “nearly $8m in lost revenue”.

Arnold, J. J. & Yüce, Ö. “Black Swan Farming using Cost of Delay”, authors' repost, blackswanfarming.com: on average 150 days to get value out of the pipeline before October 2010; 24 % of requirements took over a year.

Smith, W. E. “Various optimizers for single-stage production.” Naval Research Logistics Quarterly 3 (1956): 59–66. doi:10.1002/nav.3800030106. Ordering by weight ÷ processing time minimises total weighted completion time.
honest: The three features are a declared teaching object: stated values (£200k, £100k and £50k a month; 3, 1 and 2 months of work), not data. Real cost of delay is an estimate, and it is rarely a flat line per month: deadlines and closing windows change its shape.

Value ÷ duration is exactly the best order only for one team doing one item at a time with roughly linear delay costs. Maersk's $200,000 a week is the company's own estimate of lost revenue, not an audited figure; the 38 waiting weeks are drawn as one run, but the source does not give their calendar order.

tryit.title: Try it
tryit.note: Change the values and durations; the six orders are recounted with the same rule (value a month × the month it ships).
